{{NYCS 168th|time=bullets}} to [[168th Street (New York City Subway)|168th Street]]
{{NYCS Broadway-Seventh north|time=bullets}} to [[181st Street (IRT Broadway–Seventh Avenue Line)|181st Street]], [[191st Street (IRT Broadway–Seventh Avenue Line)|191st Street]], or [[Dyckman Street (IRT Broadway–Seventh Avenue Line)|Dyckman Street]]
'''[[New York City Bus|Bus]]''': {{NYC bus link|M2|M3|M98|M100|M101|Bx3|Bx6|Bx6 SBS|Bx11|Bx13|Bx35|Bx36}} |embedded = {{Infobox historic site | embed = yes | designation1 = NYCL | designation1_date = June 26, 2007{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2007|ps=.|p=1}} | designation1_number = 2237 | designation1_free1name = Designated entity | designation1_free1value = Bathhouse facade and pool }} }} '''Highbridge Park''' is a public park on the western bank of the [[Harlem River]] in [[Washington Heights, Manhattan|Washington Heights]], [[Manhattan]], [[New York City]]. It stretches between [[155th Street (Manhattan)|155th Street]] and [[Dyckman Street (Manhattan)|Dyckman Street]] in [[Upper Manhattan]]. The park is operated by the [[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]]. The City maintains the southern half of the park, while the northern half is maintained by the non-profit [[New York Restoration Project]].{{cite web|url=https://www.nyrp.org/green-spaces/park-details/highbridge-park|title=Highbridge Park|website=New York Restoration Project|access-date=January 7, 2019|archive-date=January 9, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190109012032/https://www.nyrp.org/green-spaces/park-details/highbridge-park|url-status=live}}{{cite web|url=https://ny.curbed.com/2015/6/25/9946618/as-high-bridge-reopens-a-neglected-park-remains-in-its-shadow|title=As High Bridge Reopens, a Neglected Park Remains in Its Shadow|author=Nathan Kensinger|work=Curbed New York|date=June 25, 2015|access-date=January 7, 2019|archive-date=January 9, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190109011940/https://ny.curbed.com/2015/6/25/9946618/as-high-bridge-reopens-a-neglected-park-remains-in-its-shadow|url-status=dead}} Prominent in the park are the Manhattan end of the [[High Bridge (New York City)|High Bridge]], the High Bridge Water Tower, and the Highbridge Play Center. ==History== Highbridge Park derives its name from New York City’s oldest standing bridge, the [[High Bridge (New York City)|High Bridge]] (1848), which was built to carry the Old [[Croton Aqueduct]] over the [[Harlem River]]. From the 17th to the 19th centuries, the area was sparsely populated with scattered farms and private estates. During the [[American Revolution]], General [[George Washington]] used the [[Morris-Jumel Mansion]], adjacent to the southern end of the park near Edgecombe Avenue and West 160th Street, as his headquarters in September and October 1776.{{cite web |title=Highbridge Park |url=http://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/highbridgepark/highlights/7732 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110919014621/http://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/highbridgepark/highlights/7732 |archive-date=September 19, 2011 |access-date=December 27, 2011 |work=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation}} ===Establishment=== The [[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation|New York City Department of Public Parks]] acquired a {{convert|2.25|mi|adj=on}} strip of land on the Harlem River between 155th and Dyckman Streets in May 1884. Afterward, several commissioners were appointed to assess the value of existing land lots within the park.{{cite news |date=9 Mar 1886 |title=The Courts: No High Bridge Park Judge Barrett Decides All the Proceeding in the Matter Void |page=3 |work=New-York Tribune |issn=1941-0646 |id={{ProQuest|573283451}}}} Local landowners complained about a New York state law that would force them to pay for half of the park's assessed value.{{Cite news |date=1886-06-08 |title=The Police Bill Signed; an Additional Force Authorized for New-york. Hearings on the Canal, Dock Commission, Washington Market, and High Bridge Park Bills. |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1886/06/08/archives/the-police-bill-signed-an-additional-force-authorized-for-newyork.html |access-date=2023-09-19 |issn=0362-4331}} A [[New York Supreme Court]] judge halted the project in 1886 following disputes over property appraisals.{{Cite news |date=1886-03-09 |title=No High Bridge Park at Present |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1886/03/09/archives/no-high-bridge-park-at-present.html |access-date=2023-09-20 |issn=0362-4331}} The park hosted the 1887 [[USA Cross Country Championships]].{{cite web |title=The Accurate Database of U.S. National Champions |url=http://www.therealxc.com |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180914184134/http://www.therealxc.com/ |archive-date=September 14, 2018 |access-date=September 14, 2018 |publisher=therealxc.com}} In February 1888, [[Samuel Parsons|Samuel Parsons Jr.]] and [[Calvert Vaux]] were ordered to prepare plans for Highbridge Park, with a main entrance at 159th Street.{{Cite news |date=1888-02-22 |title=The High Bridge Park. |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1888/02/22/archives/the-high-bridge-park.html |access-date=2023-09-20 |issn=0362-4331}} That June, the secretary of the city's Board of Street Opening was asked to prepare a resolution setting the park's northern and southern borders at 186th and 155th Streets, respectively.{{Cite news |date=1888-06-16 |title=The Cost of Relieving Broadway |pages=3 |work=New-York Tribune |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/new-york-tribune-the-cost-of-relieving-b/132091630/ |access-date=2023-09-20}} The borders were revised in December 1888 to encompass the land between [[Tenth Avenue (Manhattan)|Tenth (Amsterdam) Avenue]] to the west and the Harlem River to the east.{{cite news |date=8 Dec 1888 |title=City and Suburban News: New-york. Brooklyn. Westchester County. Staten Island. New-jersey. |page=3 |work=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 |id={{ProQuest|94653565}}}}{{Cite news |date=1888-12-08 |title=Jottings About Town |pages=2 |work=The Sun |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-sun-jottings-about-town/132092644/ |access-date=2023-09-20}}[[File:Photomechanical print of the Harlem River Speedway in the early 20th century.jpg|thumb|left|Photo-mechanical print of the Harlem River Speedway in the early 20th century showing river access from Highbridge Park]]Three men were appointed in April 1889 to appraise 1,976 lots on the site;{{Cite news |date=1889-04-02 |title=Mr. Cleveland a Commissioner. |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1889/04/02/archives/mr-cleveland-a-commissioner.html |access-date=2023-09-20 |issn=0362-4331}}{{Cite news |date=1889-04-01 |title=Grover Honored |pages=1 |work=The Evening World |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-evening-world-grover-honored/132091932/ |access-date=2023-09-20}} one of the appointees, former U.S. President [[Grover Cleveland]], declined the position.{{Cite news |date=1889-04-17 |title=Mr. Cleveland Declines. |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1889/04/17/archives/mr-cleveland-declines.html |access-date=2023-09-20 |issn=0362-4331}} Property owners continued to oppose the new park,{{Cite news |date=1889-08-04 |title=Acquiring the New Parks; One a Boon and the Other a Burden. Property Owners Will Make a Strong Fight Against the Proposed High Bridge Park. |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1889/08/04/archives/acquiring-the-new-parks-one-a-boon-and-the-other-a-burden-property.html |access-date=2023-09-20 |issn=0362-4331}} speaking out against a proposed northward extension to Dyckman Street that would have cost $2.5 million.{{cite news |date=10 Sep 1889 |title=Against Extending High Bridge Park |page=7 |work=New-York Tribune |issn=1941-0646 |id={{ProQuest|573487885}}}} In December 1889, the Board of Street Opening formally decided to reduce the park from {{convert|79|to|52.62|acre}}, running only from 170th to 181st Street.{{Cite news |date=1889-12-07 |title=High Bridge Park Reduced |pages=3 |work=Yonkers Statesman |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/yonkers-statesman-high-bridge-park-reduc/132093198/ |access-date=2023-09-20}}{{Cite news |date=1889-12-07 |title=Area of High Bridge Park. |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1889/12/07/archives/area-of-high-bridge-park.html |access-date=2023-09-20 |issn=0362-4331}} The majority of the new park, approximately {{convert|30|acre}}, was to incorporate the original High Bridge Park on the same site. The area between 190th and 192nd Streets was occupied by the [[Fort George Amusement Park]], a [[trolley park]]/[[amusement park]], from 1895 to 1914; its site is now a seating area in Highbridge Park.{{cite web |last=Martens |first=Victoria |date=August 1, 2019 |title=Fort George Amusement Park |url=https://www.mcny.org/story/fort-george-amusement-park |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190902034413/https://www.mcny.org/story/fort-george-amusement-park |archive-date=September 2, 2019 |access-date=September 2, 2019 |website=Museum of the City of New York}} A racetrack for horses, the [[Harlem River Speedway]], was opened along the riverbank of the park in 1898.{{Cite news |date=July 3, 1898 |title=Harlem Speedway Opened; Pronounced by Horsemen to be the Finest Driveway for Light Speeding in the Country |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1898/07/03/archives/harlem-speedway-opened-pronounced-by-horsemen-to-be-the-finest.html |access-date=September 15, 2017 |issn=0362-4331}} ===20th century=== ==== Early 20th century ==== [[File:Winter, High Bridge Park by George Benjamin Luks, 1912-13, High Museum of Art.jpg|thumb|left|Highbridge Park in winter, c. 1912, by [[George Benjamin Luks]]]]The cliffside area from West 181st Street to Dyckman Street was acquired in 1902, and the parcel including Fort George Hill was acquired in 1928. In 1934 the Department of Parks obtained the Highbridge Tower and the site of the old [[Highbridge Reservoir]]. By the early years of the 20th century, upper-middle class New Yorkers would promenade along the wide boardwalks in top hats and bustles. The park provided access to the [[Harlem River]] and places for horseback riding and other outdoor sports. By the 1920s dirt and other materials from the build-up of the new [[Washington Heights, Manhattan|Washington Heights]] neighborhood threatened to ruin the nascent park; a harbinger of bad times to befall the park.{{cite news|title=Landslide Threatens Highbridge Park|url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1922/04/02/102993387.pdf|newspaper=The New York Times|date=April 2, 1922|access-date=December 27, 2011|archive-date=May 10, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220510130956/https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1922/04/02/102993387.pdf|url-status=live}} ==== Works Progress Administration renovation ==== In 1934, mayor [[Fiorello H. La Guardia]] nominated [[Robert Moses]] to become commissioner of a unified [[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]]. At the time, the United States was experiencing the [[Great Depression]]; immediately after La Guardia won the [[1933 New York City mayoral election|1933 election]], Moses began to write "a plan for putting 80,000 men to work on 1,700 relief projects".{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2007|ps=.|pp=4–5}}{{harvnb|ps=.|Rodgers|1952|p=82}} By the time he was in office, several hundred such projects were underway across the city.{{harvnb|ps=.|Rodgers|1952|p=84}} Moses was especially interested in creating new pools and other bathing facilities, such as those in [[Jacob Riis Park]], [[Jones Beach State Park|Jones Beach]], and [[Orchard Beach (Bronx)|Orchard Beach]].{{Caro: The Power Broker|page=456}} He devised a list of 23 pools around the city, including one at Highbridge Park.{{Cite news|date=July 23, 1934|title=23 Bathing Pools Planned by Moses; Nine to Be Begun in a Month to Meet Shortage of Facilities Caused by Pollution|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1934/07/23/archives/23-bathing-pools-planned-by-moses-nine-to-be-begun-in-a-month-to.html|access-date=August 9, 2019|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=August 9, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190809035319/https://www.nytimes.com/1934/07/23/archives/23-bathing-pools-planned-by-moses-nine-to-be-begun-in-a-month-to.html|url-status=live}}{{Cite press release|title=Public Swimming Facilities in New York City.|date=1934-07-23|publisher=New York City Department of Parks and Recreation|access-date=2021-01-06|page=3 (PDF p. 30)|url=http://nyc.gov/html/records/pdf/govpub/41861934_press_releases_part1.pdf|archive-date=January 8, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210108104839/http://nyc.gov/html/records/pdf/govpub/41861934_press_releases_part1.pdf|url-status=live}} The pools would be built using funds from the [[Works Progress Administration]] (WPA), a federal agency created as part of the [[New Deal]] to combat the Depression's negative effects.{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/35042789/|title=City to Construct 9 Pools To Provide Safe Swimming|date=July 23, 1934|work=New York Daily News|access-date=August 18, 2019|page=8|via=newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=May 9, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220509134446/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/35042789/city-to-construct-9-pools-to-provide/|url-status=live}} Eleven of these pools were to be designed concurrently and open in 1936. Moses, along with the architects [[Aymar Embury II]] and [[Gilmore David Clarke]], created a common design for these proposed aquatic centers. Each location was to have distinct pools for diving, swimming, and wading; bleachers and viewing areas; and bathhouses with locker rooms that could be used as gymnasiums. The pools were to have several common features, such as a minimum {{Convert|55|yd|m|abbr=|adj=on}} length, underwater lighting, heating, and filtration, all constructed using inexpensive materials. To fit the requirement for efficiency and low-cost construction, each building would be built using elements of the [[Streamline Moderne]] and [[Classical architecture|Classical]] architectural styles. The buildings would also be near "comfort stations", additional playgrounds, and spruced-up landscapes.{{cite web | title=History of Parks' Swimming Pools | publisher=New York City Department of Parks and Recreation | url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/about/history/pools | access-date=2021-01-15 | archive-date=January 17, 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210117002610/https://www.nycgovparks.org/about/history/pools | url-status=live }}{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2007|ps=.|p=6}}{{Cite news|last=Shattuck|first=Kathryn|date=2006-08-14|title=Big Chill of '36: Show Celebrates Giant Depression-Era Pools That Cool New York|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/08/14/arts/design/big-chill-of-36-show-celebrates-giant-depressionera-pools-that.html|url-status=live|access-date=2021-01-08|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=January 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210110031731/https://www.nytimes.com/2006/08/14/arts/design/big-chill-of-36-show-celebrates-giant-depressionera-pools-that.html}} Construction for some of the 11 pools began that October,{{Cite news|last=|first=|date=October 4, 1934|title=Park Work Is Begun on 2 Bathing Pools; Construction Under Way at High Bridge and Hamilton Fish -- 7 Others to Be Started Soon|language=en-US|page=48|work=The New York Times|url=http://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1934/10/04/93645601.pdf|url-status=live|access-date=January 13, 2021|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=May 9, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220509134446/http://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1934/10/04/93645601.html?pdf_redirect=true&site=false}} with work commencing on the Highbridge and [[Hamilton Fish Park|Hamilton Fish]] Pools. Highbridge Park had been among the first pool sites to be selected, having been announced by ''The New York Times'' in April 1934.{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1934/04/05/archives/moses-to-get-two-unneeded-reservoirs-as-sites-for-stadium-and.html|title=Moses to Get Two Unneeded Reservoirs As Sites for Stadium and Swimming Pool|date=April 5, 1934|work=The New York Times|access-date=August 20, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=August 20, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190820025542/https://www.nytimes.com/1934/04/05/archives/moses-to-get-two-unneeded-reservoirs-as-sites-for-stadium-and.html|url-status=live}} By mid-1936, ten of the eleven WPA funded pools were completed and were being opened at a rate of one per week. The Highbridge Pool was the fifth of these pools to open,{{cite magazine|author1-link=Marta Gutman|last=Gutman|first=Marta|date=November 1, 2008|title=Race, Place, and Play: Robert Moses and the WPA Swimming Pools in New York City|magazine=Journal of the Society of Architectural Historians|publisher=University of California Press|volume=67|issue=4|page=555|doi=10.1525/jsah.2008.67.4.532|issn=0037-9808}}{{efn|The pools opened in the following chronological order: [[Hamilton Fish Park]], [[Thomas Jefferson Park]], [[Astoria Park]], [[Tompkinsville Pool]], Highbridge Park, [[Sunset Park (Brooklyn park)|Sunset Park]], [[Crotona Park]], [[McCarren Park]], [[Betsy Head Park]], [[Jackie Robinson Park|Colonial Park]], and [[Red Hook Park]].}} being opened on July 14, 1936.{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1936/07/13/archives/pool-opens-tomorrow-la-guardia-and-moses-to-speak-at-highbridge.html|title=Pool Opens Tomorrow; La Guardia and Moses to Speak at Highbridge Ceremony.|date=July 13, 1936|work=The New York Times|access-date=August 20, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=August 20, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190820025545/https://www.nytimes.com/1936/07/13/archives/pool-opens-tomorrow-la-guardia-and-moses-to-speak-at-highbridge.html|url-status=live}} The complex included a {{Convert|166|by|288|ft|abbr=|adj=on}} main pool and {{Convert|166|by|288|ft|abbr=|adj=on}} wading pool.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2007|ps=.|p=7}} ====Later 20th century==== [[File:Stone steps at High Bridge, New York City (1886).jpg|thumb|left|250px|Grand staircase, later cut by the vehicular ramp for the [[Trans-Manhattan Expressway]]]]In 1940, Moses turned portions of the Speedway into the [[Harlem River Drive]], a 6-lane highway from the Manhattan end of the [[Triborough Bridge]] at [[125th Street (Manhattan)|125th Street]], to the tunnels under Manhattan to the [[George Washington Bridge]]. New fences blocked public recreational access to the riverfront. It was this series of actions, according to Parks & Recreation Commissioner Adrian Benepe, that "ruined" the park.{{cite news|title=Parks Even the Parks Dept. Won't Claim|first=Timothy|last=Williams|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/07/06/nyregion/06parks.html|newspaper=The New York Times|date=July 6, 2005|access-date=December 27, 2011|archive-date=December 18, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141218190016/http://www.nytimes.com/2005/07/06/nyregion/06parks.html|url-status=live}} The Highbridge Play Center bathhouse was restored in the 1960s, during which the original murals by Charles Clarke were destroyed or covered over.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2007|ps=.|p=8}} The {{Convert|1200|ft|m|adj=mid|-long}}, {{Convert|116|ft|m|adj=mid|-tall}} High Bridge walkway was closed to regular public use around 1970.{{cite web|url=http://www.nycgovparks.org/park-features/northern-manhattan-parks/high-bridge-coalition/history |title=History of The High Bridge |work=NYC Dept. of Parks & Recreation |access-date=December 27, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120510151156/http://www.nycgovparks.org/park-features/northern-manhattan-parks/high-bridge-coalition/history |archive-date=May 10, 2012}} The controversial '[[Daisy (advertisement)|Daisy Girl]]' [[political advertisement]] was filmed in Highbridge Park in the summer of 1964.{{cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2014/09/07/daisy-girl-political-ad-still-haunting-50-years-later/15246667/|title=The 'Daisy Girl' political ad still haunting 50 years later|newspaper=USA Today|first=Dan|last=Novicki|date=2014-09-07|access-date=2021-08-14|archive-date=May 11, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200511192957/https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2014/09/07/daisy-girl-political-ad-still-haunting-50-years-later/15246667/|url-status=live}} By the 1970s, Highbridge Park and other city parks were in poor condition following the [[1975 New York City fiscal crisis]]. Particularly in Highbridge Park, large sections set aside as natural areas, had been taken over by homeless people who built permanent shacks made of sheet metal and steel pipes driven into the earth. Prostitutes, drug dealers and drug users frequented the park. NYC Parks commenced a project to restore the pools in several parks in 1977, including at Highbridge Park, for whose restoration the agency set aside an estimated $5.8 million.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2007|ps=.|p=10}} These projects were not carried out due to a lack of money. By March 1981, NYC Parks had only 2,900 employees in its total staff, less than 10 percent of the 30,000 present when Moses was parks commissioner.{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1981/03/15/nyregion/parks-department-to-start-hiring-for-first-time-since-fiscal-crisis.html|title=Parks Department to Start Hiring for First Time Since Fiscal Crisis|last=Carmody|first=Deirdre|date=March 15, 1981|work=The New York Times|access-date=August 9, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=August 9, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190809191156/https://www.nytimes.com/1981/03/15/nyregion/parks-department-to-start-hiring-for-first-time-since-fiscal-crisis.html|url-status=live}} In 1982, the NYC Parks budget increased greatly, enabling the agency to carry out $76 million worth of restoration projects by year's end; among these projects was the restoration of the Highbridge Park pool.{{Cite news|title=City to Start Repairing Three of Its Swimming Pools|last=Carmody|first=Deirdre|date=June 25, 1982|work=The New York Times|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|id={{ProQuest|121985503}}}} The play center and pool were completely renovated over a three-year period following a design by architect [[Stephen B. Jacobs]]. The play center reopened on June 14, 1985.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2007|ps=.|p=9}} NYC Parks continued to face financial shortfalls in the coming years, and the pools retained a reputation for high crime. In June 1984, a man set fire to the Highbridge Tower roof before jumping to his death.{{Cite news|author-link=Christopher Gray (architectural historian)|last=Gray|first=Christopher|date=October 9, 1988|title=Streetscapes: The High Bridge Water Tower; Fire-Damaged Landmark To Get $900,000 Repairs|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/10/09/realestate/streetscapes-high-bridge-water-tower-fire-damaged-landmark-get-900000-repairs.html|access-date=January 4, 2021|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=September 1, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200901172331/https://www.nytimes.com/1988/10/09/realestate/streetscapes-high-bridge-water-tower-fire-damaged-landmark-get-900000-repairs.html|url-status=live}} By the mid-1980s, Highbridge had become so degraded that during a manual cleanup in 1986, 250 tons of garbage and 25 auto wrecks were removed, but garbage again began to fill the park within a matter of days.{{cite news |last=Hellman |first=Peter |date=May 28, 1999 |title=Bette Midler Was Here: A Park Gets a Second Act |newspaper=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/05/28/arts/bette-midler-was-here-a-park-gets-a-second-act.html |url-status=live |access-date=December 27, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150527105538/http://www.nytimes.com/1999/05/28/arts/bette-midler-was-here-a-park-gets-a-second-act.html |archive-date=May 27, 2015}} For the summer of 1991, mayor David Dinkins had planned to close all 32 outdoor pools in the city, a decision that was only reversed after a $2 million donation from a trust created upon the death of real estate developer [[Sol Goldman]]{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1991/05/16/nyregion/donation-will-keep-32-public-pools-open.html|title=Donation Will Keep 32 Public Pools Open|date=May 16, 1991|work=The New York Times|access-date=August 9, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=August 9, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190809191146/https://www.nytimes.com/1991/05/16/nyregion/donation-will-keep-32-public-pools-open.html|url-status=live}} and $1.8 million from other sources. Additionally, in the 1990s, a practice called "whirlpooling" became common in New York City pools such as Highbridge Park, in which women would be inappropriately fondled by teenage boys.{{Cite news|last=Marriott|first=Michel|date=July 7, 1993|title=A Menacing Ritual Is Called Common in New York Pools|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/07/07/nyregion/a-menacing-ritual-is-called-common-in-new-york-pools.html|access-date=January 18, 2021|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=August 9, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190809191148/https://www.nytimes.com/1993/07/07/nyregion/a-menacing-ritual-is-called-common-in-new-york-pools.html|url-status=live}}{{cite news|date=July 11, 1994|title=Deep at City Pool; Sex harass is pervasive|first=Lauren|last=Terrazzano|pages=[https://www.newspapers.com/clip/34725131/ 7], [https://www.newspapers.com/clip/67963278/ 20]|work=New York Daily News|via=newspapers.com {{open access}}}} By the turn of the century, crimes such as sexual assaults had decreased in parks citywide due to increased security. The condition of Highbridge Park has gotten better, and it is no longer a haven for petty crime and other illegal activities. In November 1991, the water tower was restored. The [[New York Restoration Project]], chaired by [[Bette Midler]], has been working since 1999 to restore the park.{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/05/28/arts/bette-midler-was-here-a-park-gets-a-second-act.html|title=Bette Midler Was Here: A Park Gets a Second Act|last=Hellman|first=Peter|date=May 28, 1999|work=The New York Times|access-date=August 20, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=September 12, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170912034300/http://www.nytimes.com/1999/05/28/arts/bette-midler-was-here-a-park-gets-a-second-act.html|url-status=live}} The park also received a renovation in 1996, which included a $305,000 pool filtration system and a $445,000 renovation of heating and ventilation in the pool area. ===21st century=== On May 19, 2007, the first legal mountain bike trails and dirt jumps in New York City were opened in Highbridge Park. New York City Mountain Bike Association, working with NYC Parks & Recreation, and the International Mountain Bicycling Association (IMBA), worked to design and install the trails; the opening weekend featured a festival and cross-country mountain bike race.{{cite web|url=http://www.nycgovparks.org/downloads/highbridge_capital_projects.pdf|title=Highbridge Park Projects|work=NYC Dept. of Parks & Recreation|date=February 11, 2010|access-date=December 27, 2011|archive-date=May 10, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220510130955/http://www.nycgovparks.org/downloads/highbridge_capital_projects.pdf|url-status=live}}{{cite news|title=Highbridge Trails, NYC's First Mountain Bike Trail|first=Jen|last=Chung|url=http://gothamist.com/2007/05/15/map_of_the_day_113.php|work=Gothamist|date=May 15, 2007|access-date=December 27, 2011|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090612065345/http://gothamist.com/2007/05/15/map_of_the_day_113.php|archive-date=June 12, 2009}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/news/daily-plant?id=20111|title=The Daily Plant : NYC Parks|website=www.nycgovparks.org|access-date=August 20, 2019|archive-date=June 23, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210623194802/https://www.nycgovparks.org/news/daily-plant?id=20111|url-status=live}} Around 2010, the waterfront Speedway was rehabilitated and reopened as the Harlem River portion of the [[Manhattan Waterfront Greenway]]. By late 2011, despite the efforts of both the NYRP and NYC Parks, the infrastructure of the park had decayed significantly.{{cite web|url=http://www.nyrp.org/Parks_and_Gardens/Parks/Highbridge_Park|title=Highbridge Park|work=New York Restoration Project|access-date=December 27, 2011|archive-date=March 7, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120307002642/http://www.nyrp.org/Parks_and_Gardens/Parks/Highbridge_Park|url-status=live}} The city announced plans for a skatepark under the Hamilton Bridge in 2013,{{cite web|url=https://www.nydailynews.com/new-york/manhattan/biggest-skate-park-coming-washington-heights-article-1.1377376|title=Washington Heights to get biggest skateboard park in the entire city|last=Barron|first=Laignee|date=June 19, 2013|website=nydailynews.com|access-date=August 20, 2019|archive-date=August 20, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190820152404/https://www.nydailynews.com/new-york/manhattan/biggest-skate-park-coming-washington-heights-article-1.1377376|url-status=live}} and it opened the following year.{{cite web|url=https://ny.curbed.com/2015/6/25/9946618/as-high-bridge-reopens-a-neglected-park-remains-in-its-shadow|title=As High Bridge Reopens, a Neglected Park Remains in Its Shadow|last=Kensinger|first=Nathan|date=June 25, 2015|website=Curbed NY|access-date=August 20, 2019|archive-date=June 4, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190604192458/https://ny.curbed.com/2015/6/25/9946618/as-high-bridge-reopens-a-neglected-park-remains-in-its-shadow|url-status=dead}} The city also announced plans for an ice-skating rink in 2014.{{cite web|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20160429/washington-heights/highbridge-park-ice-rink-plan-dropped-after-no-one-wanted-run-it|title=Highbridge Park Ice Rink Plan Dropped After No One Wanted to Run it|last=Pichardo|first=Carolina|date=April 29, 2016|website=DNAinfo New York|access-date=August 20, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190820152421/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20160429/washington-heights/highbridge-park-ice-rink-plan-dropped-after-no-one-wanted-run-it/|archive-date=August 20, 2019|url-status=dead}} A citizen-driven restoration movement culminated in a grant from the [[Bloomberg administration]] to repair the bridge and make some other improvements. The restored bridge was reopened on June 9, 2015.{{cite web |url=http://www.myfoxny.com/story/29272769/high-bridge-reopens |title=High Bridge reopens to bikes, pedestrians |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150728224202/http://www.myfoxny.com/story/29272769/high-bridge-reopens |archive-date=July 28, 2015 |website=MyFox TV}} However, the park itself still faced several problems. A writer for ''Curbed NY'' observed that there were homeless encampments under the Harlem River Drive, and that much of the park south of [[Washington Bridge (Harlem River)|Washington Bridge]] remained overgrown. In contrast, the NYRP-maintained northern section of the park was extremely clean. In 2016, about $30 million in funding was allocated for further improvements to the park's recreational facilities as part of the city's Anchor Parks program.{{Cite news|last=Neuman|first=William|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/08/19/nyregion/5-neglected-new-york-city-parks-to-get-150-million-for-upgrades.html|title=5 Neglected New York City Parks to Get $150 Million for Upgrades|date=August 18, 2016|work=The New York Times|access-date=October 14, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=October 14, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191014174905/https://www.nytimes.com/2016/08/19/nyregion/5-neglected-new-york-city-parks-to-get-150-million-for-upgrades.html|url-status=live}}{{Cite news |last=Krisel |first=Brendan |date=August 18, 2016 |title=City to Invest in Highbridge Park |url=https://patch.com/new-york/washington-heights-inwood/city-invest-30-million-improvements-highbridge-park |publisher=[[Patch Media|Washington Heights Media]] |access-date=June 21, 2018 |archive-date=June 21, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180621143414/https://patch.com/new-york/washington-heights-inwood/city-invest-30-million-improvements-highbridge-park |url-status=live }} At the time, NYC Parks postponed plans for an ice-skating rink due to a lack of interest. The first phase of Highbridge Park's renovations started in December 2018. This entailed upgrades to lighting and paths, cleanup of a 10-block section of the park, restoration of the "Grand Staircase", creation of a "welcome garden" at Dyckman Street, and creation of an ADA-accessible entrance plaza at 184th Street.{{cite web|url=https://patch.com/new-york/washington-heights-inwood/city-breaks-ground-30m-highbridge-park-renovation-project|title=City Breaks Ground On $30M Highbridge Park Renovation Project|last=Krisel|first=Brendan|date=December 20, 2018|website=Washington Heights-Inwood, NY Patch|access-date=August 20, 2019|archive-date=August 20, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190820152404/https://patch.com/new-york/washington-heights-inwood/city-breaks-ground-30m-highbridge-park-renovation-project|url-status=live}} The second phase, which started in July 2019, included restoration of the water tower and the Adventure Playground at 164th Street.{{cite web|url=https://patch.com/new-york/washington-heights-inwood/work-begins-second-phase-30m-highbridge-park-renovation|title=Work Begins On Second Phase Of $30M Highbridge Park Renovation|last=Krisel|first=Brendan|date=July 15, 2019|website=Washington Heights-Inwood, NY Patch|access-date=August 20, 2019|archive-date=August 20, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190820152406/https://patch.com/new-york/washington-heights-inwood/work-begins-second-phase-30m-highbridge-park-renovation|url-status=live}} [[File:Highbridge Park brush fire 30.jpg|thumb|Firefighters putting out a brush fire in 2024]] 10–15 acres of dense brush caught fire in November 2024, as part of a [[2024 Northeastern United States wildfires|series of wildfires in the Northeast United States]] due to a drought. For many hours, smoke from it billowed over [[Harlem River Drive]]. The section that burned is steep, dense, and without much water.{{Cite news |date=November 19, 2024 |title=Brush fire in Washington Heights under control, FDNY says |url=https://abc7ny.com/post/fdny-battling-brush-fire-harlem-amid-drought-warning-nyc/15560470/ |access-date=November 21, 2024 |work=[[WABC-TV]]}}{{Cite news |last=Reid |first=Alecia |date=November 19, 2024 |title=Crews battle large brush fire in Washington Heights park |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/washington-heights-park-brush-fire/ |access-date=November 19, 2024 |work=[[CBS News]]}}{{Cite news |last=Flanagan |first=Jacob |date=November 19, 2024 |title=Washington Heights brush fire under control: FDNY |url=https://www.fox5ny.com/news/firefighters-battling-brush-fire-harlem |access-date=November 19, 2024 |work=[[WNYW]]}} ==Attractions and facilities== === Playgrounds === There are six playgrounds in Highbridge Park:{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/highbridge-park/facilities/playgrounds|title=Highbridge Park Playgrounds : NYC Parks|date=June 26, 1939|website=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation|access-date=August 20, 2019|archive-date=July 18, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190718081615/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/highbridge-park/facilities/playgrounds|url-status=live}} * Adventure Playground, at the intersection of 164th Street and Edgecombe Avenue. It was created in 1973, emulating the concept of [[Adventure playground|adventure playgrounds]] in Europe, and was renovated again in 1989 and 2017.{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/highbridge-park/highlights/11939|title=Highbridge Park Highlights - Adventure Playground : NYC Parks|date=June 26, 1939|website=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation|access-date=August 20, 2019|archive-date=July 18, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190718081303/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/highbridge-park/highlights/11939|url-status=live}} * CPF Playground, at 173rd Street near the pool * Fort George Playground, at the intersection of Fort George Avenue and St. Nicholas Avenue. It was named after [[Fort George, New York|Fort George]] and was formerly the site of [[Fort George Amusement Park]] before it was destroyed in 1914. The playground was acquired by NYC Parks in 1928 and restored in 1999.{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/highbridge-park/highlights/12317|title=Highbridge Park Highlights - Fort George Playground : NYC Parks|date=June 26, 1939|website=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation|access-date=August 20, 2019|archive-date=July 18, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190718082120/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/highbridge-park/highlights/12317|url-status=live}} * Quisqueya Playground, at the intersection of 180th Street and Amsterdam Avenue. The name "Quisqueya", honoring the local Dominican community, means "cradle of life" which was a native name for [[Hispaniola]]. The playground was created in 1934 and restored in 1998.{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/highbridge-park/highlights/12751|title=Highbridge Park Highlights - Quisqueya Playground : NYC Parks|date=June 26, 1939|website=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation|access-date=August 20, 2019|archive-date=August 20, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190820163945/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/highbridge-park/highlights/12751|url-status=live}} * Sunken Playground, at the intersection of 167th Street and Edgecombe Avenue * Wallenberg Playground, at the intersection of 189th Street and Amsterdam Avenue ===High Bridge Water Tower=== {{multiple image | align = right | direction = horizontal | image1 = 2014 High Bridge Water Tower from below north.jpg | width1 = 116 | caption1 = The tower, seen from the north | image2 = 2014 High Bridge Water Tower top from below southwest.jpg | width2 = 185 | caption2 = The top of the tower, seen from the south | image3 = High Bridge Water Tower from High Bridge span.jpg | width3 = 186 | caption3 = From mid-span of High Bridge }} The '''High Bridge Water Tower''' is in Highbridge Park between West 173rd and 174th streets, on top of the ridge at the Manhattan end of the High Bridge. The {{Convert|200|ft|m|adj=on}} octagonal tower, which was authorized by the State Legislature in 1863, was designed by [[John B. Jervis]], the engineer who supervised the bridge's and aqueduct's construction. Water was pumped up {{Convert|100|ft}} to [[Highbridge Reservoir]], a {{Convert|7|acre|ha|adj=on}} reservoir next to the tower, which then provided water to be lifted to the tower's {{Convert|47,000|gal|m3}} tank. This "high service" improved the water system's gravity pressure, necessary because of the increased use of [[flush toilet]]s.{{cite aia5|page=566}}{{Cite news |title=Streetscapes: The High Bridge Water Tower; Fire-Damaged Landmark To Get $900,000 Repairs |last=Gray |first=Christopher |author-link=Christopher Gray (architectural historian) |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/10/09/realestate/streetscapes-high-bridge-water-tower-fire-damaged-landmark-get-900000-repairs.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=October 9, 1988}} The tower's load-bearing exterior stonework was designed in a mixture of the [[Romanesque Revival architecture|Romanesque Revival]] and [[neo-Grec]] styles. [[Christopher Gray (architectural historian)|Christopher Gray]] said of the tower's design that "Its rock-faced granite gives the tower a chunky, fortified appearance, as if it were a lookout for a much larger castle complex that was never built.... The granite is competently handled, but the details are not very inspired or elegant. The tower is more picturesque than beautiful." The interior of the tower, which was never open to the public, features a wide well-detailed [[iron]] spiral staircase with six large landings and paired windows. The tower was built in 1866–1872 to help meet the ever-increasing demands on the city's water system, and the High Bridge system reached its full capacity by 1875. With the opening of the New Croton Aqueduct in 1890, the High Bridge system became less relied upon; during [[World War I]], it was completely shut down when sabotage was feared. The tower was removed from service in 1949, and it was proposed for demolition the next year to make way for a planned highway interchange between [[Harlem River Drive]] and the [[178th–179th Street Tunnels]].{{cite news |last=Price |first=Ben |date=8 Apr 1950 |title=Old Highbridge Pump Station Is Being Razed: 1888 Landmark on Site of $13,000,000 Washington Heights Highway Project |work=New York Herald Tribune |page=9 |issn=1941-0646 |id={{ProQuest|1327403687}}}} The tower was saved when [[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]] (NYC Parks) offered to take over control.{{cite web |date=November 24, 1951 |title=High Bridge Water Tower Saved as City Landmark |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1951/11/24/archives/high-bridge-water-tower-saved-as-city-landmark.html |access-date=January 9, 2026 |website=The New York Times}}{{cite news |last=Ubell |first=Earl |date=24 Nov 1951 |title=Water Tower At High Bridge Spared by City: 170-Ft. Structure Above the Harlem, Built in '66, Kept as Historical Landmark Manhattan Landmark Saved by Park Department |work=New York Herald Tribune |page=11 |issn=1941-0646 |id={{ProQuest|1326978154}}}} A [[carillon]], donated by the Altman Foundation, was installed in 1958. The tower's cupola was damaged by an arson fire in 1984. It was reconstructed, cleaned and restored in 1989–1990 by the William A. Hall Partnership. The High Bridge Water Tower underwent a 10-year, $5 million renovation during the 2010s and reopened to the public in November 2021.{{cite web |last=Richardson |first=Kemberly |date=November 3, 2021 |title=NYC's historic High Bridge Water Tower in Washington Heights reopening soon after more than a decade |url=https://abc7ny.com/high-bridge-water-tower-washington-heights-nyc-manhattan/11174023/ |access-date=November 15, 2022 |website=ABC7 New York}}{{cite web |last=Rahmanan |first=Anna |date=October 28, 2021 |title=You can tour this historic NYC tower for the first time in a decade |url=https://www.timeout.com/newyork/news/you-can-tour-this-historic-nyc-tower-for-the-first-time-in-a-decade-102821 |access-date=November 15, 2022 |website=Time Out New York}} After the water tower reopened, NYC Parks began hosting free tours of the structure.{{cite web |last=Sheidlower |first=Noah |date=March 7, 2022 |title=Go Inside NYC's High Bridge Water Tower |url=https://untappedcities.com/2022/03/07/go-inside-high-bridge-water-tower/ |access-date=November 15, 2022 |website=Untapped New York}} ===Highbridge Play Center=== The '''Highbridge Play Center''', on [[Tenth Avenue (Manhattan)|Amsterdam Avenue]] between [[172nd Street (Manhattan)|West 172nd]] and [[174th Street (Manhattan)|West 174th]] Streets, was built in 1934-36 in the [[Art Moderne]] style, during the [[Fiorello H. La Guardia|Fiorello LaGuardia administration]]. The supervising architect was [[Aymar Embury II]], and the landscape architect was [[Gilmore David Clarke|Gilmore D. Clarke]], among others. It was built on the site of the Highbridge Reservoir and features a swimming pool.{{cite nycland|page=210}} ==== Bathhouse ==== [[File:Highbridge Play Center front jeh.jpg|left|thumb|Main entrance]] The bathhouse is set on an [[ashlar]] base above the surrounding street level, while the rest of the structure is made of brick. The building is rectangular: the longer side is on a north-south axis (i.e. parallel to Amsterdam Avenue), while the shorter side is on a west-east axis (i.e. parallel to 173rd Street). Its main entrance is on an elevated, slightly projecting [[portico]] at Amsterdam Avenue and 173rd Street. Stone staircases on either side ascend to the portico. The portico itself consists of two brick towers with flagpoles, two concrete piers that carry a concrete [[architrave]], and a bronze sign with the words {{Smallcaps|highbridge play center}} at the top of the architrave. Just inside the portico, there is a circular turret with a second-story loft, overlooking the first-floor entrance. The north and south wings respectively contain the women's and men's locker rooms and are nearly identical. Both have nine windows separated by eight brick [[Pilaster|pilasters]]. The stone [[Capital (architecture)|capitals]] of the pilasters line up with the [[Lintel|lintels]] of the windows. Ramps lead from the extreme ends of each wing. The ground slopes down northward, so that the northern wing is at a higher elevation above the ground than the southern wing. The eastern facade is similar to the western facade, except that it contains entrances to both genders' respective locker rooms, as well as a bronze clock hanging from the architrave. A cellar is below the northern wing.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2007|ps=.|p=11}} ==== Pools ==== The Highbridge Pool contains two rectangular pools: a main pool to the east and a wading pool to the west. The main pool measures {{convert|228|ft}} wide by {{Convert|165|ft}} long, with the wider dimension extending north-south,{{efn|Dimensions of the main pool are alternatively given as {{convert|220|by|162|ft}}.}} and a depth of {{convert|10.5|ft}}.{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/67847266/|title=Taking the plunge|first=Lisa|last=Rein|date=1999-06-30|work=New York Daily News|access-date=2021-01-17|page=164|via=newspapers.com {{open access}}|archive-date=May 9, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220509134450/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/67847266/taking-the-plunge/|url-status=live}} The wading pool measures {{Convert|228|ft}} wide by {{convert|97|ft}} long. A {{Convert|29|ft|m|-wide|abbr=|adj=mid}} promenade surrounds the pool area on the north, south, and east sides. A set of concrete bleachers is to the north of the pool area. A short brick wall encloses the pool area, and niches along the eastern boundary provide another seating area. Just east of the pool area is a set of stairs that leads to the High Bridge. The water tower is at the northeast corner of the pool area. == Landmark designations == The High Bridge Water Tower was designated a [[New York City landmark]] by the [[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]] in 1967. The Play Center was designated a New York City landmark by the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission in 2007. The commission had also considered the pool for landmark status in 1990, along with the other ten WPA pools in the city.{{harvnb|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2007|ps=.|p=1}}{{Cite news|last=Brozan|first=Nadine|date=1990-07-30|title=A Crumbling Pool Divides a Neighborhood|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1990/07/30/nyregion/a-crumbling-pool-divides-a-neighborhood.html|access-date=2021-01-11|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=January 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210110105137/https://www.nytimes.com/1990/07/30/nyregion/a-crumbling-pool-divides-a-neighborhood.html|url-status=live}} == See also == {{commons category multi|Highbridge Park, Manhattan|High Bridge Water Tower|Highbridge Play Center|High Bridge (New York City)}} * [[List of New York City Designated Landmarks in Manhattan above 110th Street]] ==References== ===Notes=== {{notelist}} ===Citations=== {{reflist}} ===Sources=== *{{cite web|url=https://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/2237.pdf|title=Highbridge Play Center Exterior|last=Noonan|first=Theresa C.|date=June 26, 2007|publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]|ref={{harvid|Landmarks Preservation Commission|2007}}}} *{{Cite book|last=Rodgers|first=Cleveland|title=Robert Moses, Builder for Democracy|date=1952|publisher=Holt|location=New York|language=English|oclc=528489}} ==External links== * [https://web.archive.org/web/20070926223534/http://www.nycgovparks.org/sub_your_park/historical_signs/hs_historical_sign.php?id=7732 nycgovparks.org: Highbridge Park] * [https://web.archive.org/web/20060513062728/http://www.nyrp.org/theparks_highbridge.htm New York Restoration Project: Highbridge Park] * [https://web.archive.org/web/20110724234941/http://allianceprogress.org/hbpark.aspx Alliance For Progress -
